stem: What is prime cost?

options.content: Direct materials, direct labour and direct expenses
options.rationale: Correct: the total of the direct costs of production.

options.content: Direct materials and factory overheads only
options.rationale: Direct labour is also part of prime cost, and overheads are not.

options.content: The cost of production less the change in work in progress
options.rationale: That is how the cost of production is built up from factory cost.

options.content: All the costs of the business in the year
options.rationale: Prime cost includes only direct manufacturing costs.

explanation: Prime cost = raw materials consumed + direct labour + direct expenses.

stem: Which one of the following is a factory overhead?

options.rationale: Correct: it is an indirect cost of running the factory.

options.content: Wages of workers who assemble the product
options.rationale: These are direct labour and form part of prime cost.
Selling costs are not manufacturing costs.
This is a direct material.

explanation: Indirect factory costs such as machine depreciation, power and indirect wages are factory overheads.

stem: Opening inventory of raw materials US\$6,400, purchases US\$38,900, carriage inwards US\$1,500, returns outwards US\$900 and closing inventory US\$7,300. What is the cost of raw materials consumed?

options.rationale: Carriage inwards has been left out.
Returns outwards must be deducted.
Closing inventory must be deducted.

explanation: Opening + purchases + carriage inwards − returns outwards − closing inventory = 38,600.
hints: Add what came in, take away what went out or remains.

stem: How is carriage inwards treated in a manufacturing account?

options.rationale: It is part of the cost of materials, before prime cost.
It increases the cost of materials.

options.content: It is added to the cost of purchases of raw materials
options.rationale: Correct: it is part of the cost of bringing the materials to the factory.

options.content: It is charged in the statement of profit or loss as a selling cost
options.rationale: It is a cost of getting materials, not of selling goods.

explanation: Carriage inwards increases the cost of the raw materials and is included before prime cost.
hints: Does it relate to materials coming in or goods going out?

stem: Factory cost is US\$84,200. Opening work in progress is US\$5,300 and closing work in progress is US\$6,900. What is the cost of production?

options.rationale: The opening and closing work in progress have been reversed.
Correct: add the opening and deduct the closing work in progress.
The closing work in progress must be deducted.
Ignoring work in progress overstates or understates the cost of the goods completed.

hints: Opening work in progress was started last year.

stem: A factory completes 2,400 units at a cost of production of US\$93,600. What is the production cost per unit?

options.rationale: The number of units is the units completed.
The cost must be divided by the units, not multiplied.
The division is the wrong way round.

hints: Divide the cost by the number of units.

stem: Which item is NOT included in the manufacturing account?

options.rationale: This is a factory overhead.
Indirect factory wages are a factory overhead.
A per-unit royalty is a direct expense.
Correct: administration costs belong in the statement of profit or loss.

explanation: Only the costs of making the goods are in the manufacturing account.
hints: Is the cost incurred in making the goods?

stem: The factory cost is US\$110,400. At the start of the year work in progress was US\$8,200. More goods were still unfinished at the end of the year, with a value of US\$12,600. What effect does the increase in work in progress have on the cost of production?

options.content: It increases the cost of production by US\$4,400
options.rationale: A larger closing figure is deducted.

options.content: It has no effect, because work in progress is an asset
options.rationale: The change in work in progress adjusts the cost of production.

options.content: It increases the factory cost by US\$12,600
options.rationale: Factory cost is not changed; the adjustment follows it.

options.content: It reduces the cost of production by US\$4,400 to US\$106,000
options.rationale: Correct: a higher closing figure removes more cost, carrying it into next year.

explanation: Cost of production = 110,400 + 8,200 − 12,600 = 106,000, which is 4,400 less than the factory cost.
hints: Closing work in progress is deducted.

stem: The cost of production from the manufacturing account is transferred to the trading account in place of purchases.
explanation: True. The goods are made by the business, so the cost of production replaces purchases of finished goods.

stem: Factory power is part of prime cost.
explanation: False. Factory power is an overhead added after prime cost to give the factory cost.
hints: Is it a direct cost or an overhead?

stem: Match each cost of a furniture factory with its classification.

left.content: Wages of the carpenters who make the chairs

right.content: Selling cost (not in the manufacturing account)

explanation: Direct costs form prime cost; indirect factory costs are overheads; selling costs stay out.

stem: Complete the statements about the manufacturing account.

payload.template: Prime cost plus factory overheads gives {{blank:a}} cost. After adjusting for work in progress the result is the cost of {{blank:b}}, which is transferred to the {{blank:c}} account.

explanation: Factory cost, then cost of production, which goes to the trading account.

stem: Opening raw materials US\$9,200, purchases US\$52,800, carriage inwards US\$1,100, closing raw materials US\$11,300, manufacturing wages US\$31,400 and royalties on units produced US\$2,500. Calculate the prime cost.
hints: Find the raw materials consumed first.

stem: Rent of US\$21,000 is shared between factory and office on a floor area basis. The factory occupies 65% of the floor area. How much rent is a factory overhead?
explanation: 21,000 × 65% = 13,650. The remaining 7,350 is an administration expense.
workedSolution: 1. 21,000 × 65% = 13,650. The remaining 7,350 is an administration expense.

stem: Prime cost is US\$128,400, factory overheads US\$35,900, opening work in progress US\$6,100 and closing work in progress US\$4,800. Calculate the cost of production.
hints: Add opening work in progress and deduct the closing.

stem: The cost of production is US\$165,600 and 3,000 units were completed. Calculate the cost per unit, to the nearest cent.
hints: Divide the cost by the units.

stem: Name the account that is prepared to find the cost of the goods a business makes.
explanation: The manufacturing account finds the cost of production.

stem: Explain why a manufacturer prepares a manufacturing account before the trading account.

points.description: The goods are made by the business, so there is no purchase price for them
The account calculates the cost of production, which replaces purchases in the trading account
It shows the cost of materials, labour and overheads, which helps control costs

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: A manufacturer makes its goods, so it has no purchase price for them. The manufacturing account finds the cost of production, which replaces purchases in the trading account, and shows the costs that can be controlled.

explanation: One mark each for the reason, the link to the trading account and cost control.
hints: Where do the goods come from?

stem: Distinguish between prime cost and factory overheads, giving one example of each from a bakery.

points.description: Prime cost consists of direct costs (materials, labour and direct expenses)
Factory overheads are indirect costs of running the factory
Examples: flour (prime cost) and depreciation of the oven or factory power (overhead)

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: Prime cost is the total of direct materials, direct labour and direct expenses, for example flour. Factory overheads are indirect costs of running the factory, such as depreciation of the oven.

explanation: One mark for each definition and one for suitable examples.
hints: Can the cost be traced to a unit?

stem: The owner of a small manufacturer says: "Cost of production per unit rose this year, so we must be less efficient." Evaluate this statement.

points.description: Cost per unit may have risen because material prices or wages rose, not because of inefficiency
A change in the number of units produced affects the cost per unit when overheads are fixed
Look at each element (materials, labour, overheads) to find the cause
Conclusion: the statement may be true but needs analysis of the elements before action

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: Rising cost per unit might be due to higher prices of materials or wages or to fewer units being made over fixed overheads. The owner should compare each element of cost with the previous year before deciding whether efficiency has fallen.

explanation: A balanced answer separates price changes and volume changes from efficiency.
hints: What else could raise the unit cost?

stem: Chinhoyi Brick Works makes bricks. For the year ended 31 December 2025: raw materials opening inventory US\$8,400, purchases US\$41,600, carriage inwards US\$1,200, closing inventory US\$9,800; manufacturing wages US\$27,500; factory power US\$6,300; indirect factory wages US\$7,900; depreciation of kilns US\$4,200; rent US\$9,600 (60% factory); work in progress opening US\$3,100, closing US\$2,600. The factory completed 3,600 bricks.

parts.label: (a)
parts.stem: Calculate the cost of raw materials consumed.

parts.label: (c)
parts.stem: Prepare the manufacturing account for the year.

points.description: Cost of raw materials consumed 41,400 with carriage inwards included
Prime cost 68,900 (own figure)
Factory overheads listed with the factory share of rent 5,760 and total 24,160
Opening and closing work in progress added and deducted
Cost of production with heading and brackets for deductions

parts.label: (d)
parts.stem: Calculate the cost of production per brick, to the nearest cent.

parts.label: (e)
parts.stem: Where is the remaining 40% of the rent shown?

options.content: In the manufacturing account as a direct expense
options.rationale: It is not a factory cost.

options.content: In administration expenses in the statement of profit or loss
options.rationale: Correct: it relates to the office.

options.content: As a deduction from the cost of production
options.rationale: It is an expense, not a deduction.

options.content: In the statement of financial position as a prepayment
options.rationale: It is an expense of the year.

parts.explanation: The office share of a shared expense is an administration expense.

explanation: This item practises a full manufacturing account with apportionment and cost per unit.
hints: Apportion the rent first: 60% is a factory overhead.
Add opening work in progress and deduct the closing.

stem: Rudo Metalworks in Bulawayo made 2,500 units in the year ended 31 December 2025. Raw materials: opening inventory US\$12,300, purchases US\$78,000, closing inventory US\$10,500. Direct labour US\$46,000; indirect factory wages US\$11,000. Work in progress: opening US\$6,200, closing US\$7,400. Shared expenses: rent US\$15,000 (60% factory), electricity US\$9,000 (75% factory), insurance US\$4,800 (50% factory); machinery depreciation 12% on cost of US\$70,000 (factory); office equipment depreciation 10% on cost of US\$20,000. A supplier offers to supply the same units for US\$62 each.

parts.label: (a)
parts.stem: Prepare a statement apportioning the shared expenses between the factory and the office.

points.description: Rent 9,000 factory and 6,000 office
Electricity 6,750 and 2,250; insurance 2,400 and 2,400
Machinery depreciation 8,400 all factory; office equipment 2,000 all office
Totals: 26,550 factory, 12,650 office (own figures if consistent)

parts.explanation: Each total is split using the stated proportions.

parts.label: (b)
parts.explanation: Raw materials consumed 79,800; prime cost 125,800; factory overheads 11,000 + 26,550 = 37,550; factory cost 163,350; add 6,200 and deduct 7,400 = 162,150.
parts.workedSolution: 1. Raw materials consumed 79,800; prime cost 125,800; factory overheads 11,000 + 26,550 = 37,550; factory cost 163,350; add 6,200 and deduct 7,400 = 162,150.

parts.label: (c)
parts.stem: Calculate the cost of production per unit, to the nearest cent.

parts.label: (d)
parts.stem: The business adds a mark-up of 50% on the cost of production to find the selling price. Calculate the selling price per unit, to the nearest cent.

parts.label: (e)
parts.stem: Evaluate whether Rudo Metalworks should buy from the supplier instead of making the units, and advise the owner.

points.description: The supplier's price of US\$62 is below the production cost of US\$64.86, a saving of US\$2.86 per unit
The saving is not certain because some factory overheads (rent, depreciation) continue even if production stops
Only the avoidable costs should be compared, not the full cost
Non-financial factors: quality, reliability of supply, loss of skilled staff, control
Advice: do not stop production solely on the full-cost comparison; compare avoidable costs and check quality

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: The offer of US\$62 is below the production cost of US\$64.86, but some overheads such as rent and depreciation continue if production stops, so the real saving is smaller. Quality, reliability and the loss of skilled staff matter too. The owner should compare avoidable costs and check the supplier's quality before deciding.

parts.explanation: One mark each for the comparison, fixed costs, avoidable costs, non-financial factors and the advice.

explanation: This item practises apportionment, the cost of production, unit cost and a make-or-buy evaluation.
hints: Raw materials consumed = opening + purchases − closing.
